props.title: The Last American Virgin
props.initialSlug: Teen's first love leads to heartbreak in 80s LA

sections.content: The Last American Virgin (1982) stands as one of the most brutally honest teen films of the 1980s, demolishing the typical happy endings that dominated the era. While superficially similar to lighter fare like Porky's (1982) and Fast Times at Ridgemont High (1982), it takes a darker path inspired by its Israeli source film Lemon Popsicle (1978). The film follows Gary, a pizza delivery boy navigating first love, sexual awakening, and devastating heartbreak in early 1980s Los Angeles. Its unflinching portrayal of teenage pregnancy, abortion, and romantic disillusionment set it apart from its contemporary teen comedies.

sections.content: The film's lasting impact comes from its soundtrack and authentic portrayal of early 80s teen life. While movies like Valley Girl (1983) and Sixteen Candles (1984) romanticized the era, The Last American Virgin captured the gritty reality of teenage social dynamics. The new wave soundtrack featuring U2, The Police, and The Cars perfectly encapsulates the period while avoiding nostalgia. Director Boaz Davidson brought the harsh realism of his Israeli films to this American remake, creating something uniquely devastating in the teen genre.

What truly sets the film apart is its ending, which subverts every teen movie trope of its time. Unlike Pretty in Pink (1986) or Some Kind of Wonderful (1987), there's no triumphant moment where the nice guy gets the girl. Instead, it delivers one of the most emotionally crushing finales in teen cinema history, more in line with serious dramas like Lucas (1986) than its sex comedy contemporaries. sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later teen movies that dared to break from formula, like Welcome to the Dollhouse (1995) and Kids (1995). Its realistic treatment of teenage sexuality and consequences paved the way for more serious teen dramas like River's Edge (1986) and Thirteen (2003). While often overlooked in discussions of 80s teen cinema, its unflinching approach to teenage reality makes it more relevant than ever.
